A synthesis of 50 classroom studies found most were qualitative and few theoretically motivated (Mao et al., 2024). Within this framing, the library distinguishes teacher-provided feedback, peer feedback, and automated writing evaluation (AWE), and documents uptake, attention and affective response for each.

Teacher feedback anchors the comparison. Razmi and Ghane (2024) reported that Iranian male learners receiving WCF outperformed controls on writing performance and self-efficacy and showed lower writing anxiety, though the sample was small, exclusively male, and intermediate-level. Zhang and Hyland (2018) showed that teacher feedback addressed more error types than automated writing evaluation (AWE), which tended to highlight rather than correct errors; the highly engaged learner outperformed the moderately engaged one in responding to both sources. Learner preferences converge on explicit teacher input: university ESL students favoured direct correction combined with metalinguistic explanations over direct correction alone (Liu & Wu, 2019).

Experimental work indicates that feedback explicitness shapes accuracy gains and processing effort. Self-reported cognitive load was lower after direct corrections on grammatical errors than after metalinguistic codes on all errors (Bonilla López et al., 2018). Peer-mediated revision also produced meaningful score gains, although students ignored some peer comments (Li & Hebert, 2023). In an integrated approach, most students actively engaged and revised thoughtfully (Zhang and Hyland, 2021).

Automated feedback raises distinct questions of accuracy and teacher role. Teachers using Grammarly reported time savings yet still addressed lower-order concerns (Koltovskaia, 2022). Concerns persist that AI feedback lacks specificity and rhetorical insight (Hyland, 2025).

sentences: Research on written corrective feedback (WCF) in second-language (L2) writing has moved from asking whether feedback works to asking how learners engage with it.
This review synthesises the project library on uptake, attention, and affective response, distinguishing direct corrections, metalinguistic codes, and automated feedback.
It draws on experimental, case-study, and synthesis evidence, with inclusion limited to sources in the project library.
Experimental work indicates that feedback explicitness shapes both accuracy gains and processing effort.

In a randomised study of 139 low-intermediate EFL writers, Bonilla López et al. (2018) found that direct corrections and metalinguistic codes improved immediate grammatical and non-grammatical accuracy, but only direct corrections produced a long-term advantage four weeks after feedback.
Self-reported cognitive load was lower after direct corrections on grammatical errors than after metalinguistic codes on all errors (Bonilla López et al., 2018).
This suggests a trade-off: codes may demand more attention yet not yield durable gains in this population.
Affective outcomes are documented less consistently.

Razmi and Ghane (2024) reported that Iranian male learners receiving WCF outperformed controls on writing performance and self-efficacy and showed lower writing anxiety, though the sample was small, exclusively male, and intermediate-level.
Whether such gains generalise across proficiency levels and genders remains untested in the library.
Engagement research complicates the picture.

Zhang and Hyland (2018) showed that teacher feedback addressed more error types than automated writing evaluation (AWE), which tended to highlight rather than correct errors; the highly engaged learner outperformed the moderately engaged one in responding to both sources.
In an integrated approach, most students actively engaged and revised thoughtfully (Zhang and Hyland, 2021).
Peer-mediated revision also produced meaningful score gains, although students ignored some peer comments (Li & Hebert, 2023).

Automated tools are not interchangeable: ChatGPT achieved higher precision than Grammarly but lower recall, improving with prompt sophistication (Luo et al., 2025), while teachers using Grammarly reported time savings yet still addressed lower-order concerns (Koltovskaia, 2022).
A synthesis of 50 classroom studies found most were qualitative and few theoretically motivated (Mao et al., 2024), leaving the mechanisms linking feedback type to uptake and affect under-specified.
Across these studies, feedback type, learner engagement, and affective response interact, but evidence remains fragmented across small samples and single contexts.

quotes: The most noteworthy finding, however, is that the experimental group outperformed the control group in all three measures with larger effect size, as evidenced by the results of independent sample t-tests (Table 3).

Table 3 demonstrates that the experimental group outperformed the control group in terms of writing performance, as indicated by the statistically significant difference between their mean scores, M = 79.34, SD = 11.14 vs. M = 62.53, SD = 14.32, t (50) = 4.722, p < 0.05, d = 1.32.

Furthermore, the experimental group reported higher levels of writing self-efficacy, M = 51.30, SD = 7.29 compared to the control group, M = 42.15, SD = 9.64, with a statistically significant difference, t (50) = 3.858, p < 0.05, d = 1.08.

Similarly, the experimental group demonstrated a significant decrease in writing anxiety, as evidenced by their lower mean score on the posttest anxiety assessment, M = 49.96, SD = 18.75 compared to the control group, M = 71.19, SD=14.91, with a statistically significant difference, t (50) = 4.518, p < 0.05, d = 1.26.
52 EFL male students (age range of 12-18), selected among 82 students based on the Oxford Placement Test (OPT) results in an English institute, constituted the participants in this study.
Their scores ranged from 41 to 52 and were at the level B1 as measured by OPT.

First, the sample size was relatively small, with only 52 participants. Second, the study focused solely on intermediate level students who were exclusively male, with the age range limited to 12-18 years.

uncited_sentences.sentence: Research on written corrective feedback (WCF) in second-language (L2) writing increasingly examines how learners engage with feedback rather than only whether it improves accuracy.
Within this framing, the library distinguishes teacher-provided feedback, peer feedback, and automated writing evaluation (AWE), and documents uptake, attention and affective response for each.
Experimental work indicates that feedback explicitness shapes accuracy gains and processing effort.
Automated feedback raises distinct questions of accuracy and teacher role.
Affective outcomes are documented less consistently.
Across these studies, feedback type, learner engagement, and affective response interact, but evidence remains fragmented across small samples and single contexts.
